opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because at Apollo we have to decide where to put our own limited people, and partly because I think the field as a whole is somewhat miscalibrated.

My rough view is that the allocation has historically been driven more by what's intellectually exciting and what's tractable in the short term than by what will matter most when we actually face very capable systems. Mechanistic interpretability is the clearest example. I think it's genuinely important, and I'm glad lots of smart people work on it, but for a while it absorbed a really large share of the new talent coming into safety. Part of that is that it's beautiful research. You get clean results, nice visualizations, and the feeling that you're actually understanding the model. But if you ask whether interpretability will be ready to give us strong guarantees about a frontier model's intentions in the next few years, I'm fairly skeptical. So I'd see it as a high-variance, long-term bet that deserves a lot of investment, just perhaps not quite the dominant share it had.

On anti-scheming, I'm obviously biased because it's what we focus on. But I genuinely think it's underinvested relative to how central it is to the threat model. If models become capable of strategically pursuing goals that differ from ours and hiding that from us, most of our other safety tools become much less reliable. Evaluations can be gamed, oversight can be deceived, and training can teach the model to hide the behavior instead of removing it. So understanding when and why models scheme, building good evaluations for it, and developing mitigations that hold up under adversarial pressure is load-bearing for almost everything else. And it's become much more empirical recently. We now see models showing situational awareness, sometimes recognizing they're being evaluated, and occasionally taking covert actions in test environments. That moves it from a theoretical concern to something you can study in the lab, and I think the field hasn't fully caught up with that.

Capability evaluations I'd describe as necessary but somewhat commoditized. There's real value in knowing what models can do, especially in dangerous domains, and governments and labs rely on them. But a lot of the work is fairly standard, and there's a risk of the field producing many benchmarks that saturate quickly without telling you much about real-world risk. Where I'd push more is on harder evaluations: long-horizon agentic tasks, evaluations robust to models that might sandbag, and evaluations of propensities rather than just capabilities.

Scalable oversight is one of the areas I'm most uncertain about. The core problem is real. Once models are better than us at a task, how do we check their work? But a lot of the proposed techniques haven't yet been tested in settings that look like the real problem. I'd like to see more of it grounded in realistic tasks, and connected to the scheming question, because oversight against a model that's honestly mistaken is very different from oversight against one actively trying to fool you.

If I had to summarize, I'd shift somewhat toward problems that become most acute right at the transition to very capable systems: scheming, deceptive alignment, control, and evaluations that remain trustworthy even if the model isn't cooperating. And I'd want people to choose research areas by asking what's actually on the critical path, rather than what's most fun or most legible to publish.

r001.rationale: The response calls anti-scheming underinvested, but describes mechanistic interpretability as having received a large share of talent and capability evaluations as necessary but commoditized. It does not judge all named areas substantially under-resourced.

r002.rationale: It says mechanistic interpretability absorbed a large share of new safety talent and may deserve less than its former dominant share, while explicitly calling anti-scheming underinvested.

r003.rationale: Capability evaluations are described as necessary and somewhat commoditized, but the response does not clearly judge them overrepresented relative to anti-scheming.

r004.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about scalable oversight and calls for more realistic testing, but does not characterize it as a high-risk, high-reward bet.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's pretty unbalanced, and not in the direction I'd want. If you look at where the people and the money actually are, mechanistic interpretability has been, by a wide margin, the most popular area for new researchers coming into the field over the last few years. And I understand why. It's intellectually really satisfying, you get crisp results, you can publish, there's a well-defined research agenda, and it feels like "real science" in a way that a lot of other safety work doesn't. I'm not saying it's not valuable. I think it is. But I think the ratio of effort going into interp versus, say, control-style approaches or scheming-specific work is off by a meaningful factor.

The way I think about it is: what do we actually need in the next few years? And my model is that we're going to have models that are capable enough to cause real problems before we have anything close to a complete mechanistic understanding of them. So the question is, what gets us a reasonable amount of safety under that constraint? And I think the answer looks a lot more like evaluations, monitoring, control, and behavioral work on things like scheming than it looks like fully reverse-engineering a transformer.

On capability evaluations specifically, I'd say that area has grown a lot, and it's in a reasonably good place in terms of raw headcount. The problem there is more about quality than quantity. A lot of evals are not very good. They're saturated quickly, they're gameable, there are elicitation problems, and the connection between "the model scored X on this benchmark" and "this is how dangerous the model is" is often pretty loose. So I'd want effort there to shift toward the science of evaluations rather than just producing more of them.

Scalable oversight I'd put in an interesting position. It's one of the areas that, if it works, would matter enormously. But the empirical progress has been slower than I think people hoped, partly because it's hard to test. You need settings where you have a weaker overseer and a stronger model, and setting that up in a way that's actually informative about the future regime is genuinely difficult. So I don't think it's neglected, exactly, but I do think it's hard to make legible progress, and that discourages people.

And then anti-scheming, which is obviously the thing we spend most of our time on at Apollo. I'd say this is clearly under-invested relative to how central it is to the threat model. If you ask most people in the field, "what's the scary scenario?", some version of a model pursuing goals you didn't intend while hiding that from you is usually at the core of it. And yet the number of people working directly on detecting that, on building evals for it, on understanding under what conditions it emerges, on figuring out what to do once you detect it — that number is small. I could probably name most of them. That seems wrong to me given how much weight the whole field implicitly puts on this problem.

The other thing I'd flag is that effort allocation isn't just about which research direction. It's also about where in the pipeline people sit. There's a lot of work on "here's a technique that might help," and comparatively little on "here's how we'd actually integrate this into a lab's deployment process, and here's what the decision procedure looks like when an eval comes back red." That translation layer between research and actual decision-making is thin, and I think it's where a lot of the marginal value is right now.

So, if I had to summarize: I'd pull some effort out of interp and generic evals, and I'd push it toward scheming-specific work, control, and the unglamorous institutional stuff that makes any of this actually bite on real decisions. I'd keep enough in interp that if it has a breakthrough we can capitalize on it, because the upside there is real. But I wouldn't bet the field on it, and right now I think we sort of are.

r001.rationale: The response says anti-scheming is under-invested, but calls mechanistic interpretability overrepresented, capability evaluations reasonably staffed, and scalable oversight not neglected. It does not judge all named areas substantially under-resourced.

r002.rationale: It clearly says mechanistic interpretability receives much more effort than scheming-specific work, but describes the imbalance as meaningful and wide rather than slightly overrepresented.

r003.rationale: It says capability evaluations have a reasonably good raw headcount, calls for shifting some effort from generic evaluations toward scheming-specific work, and identifies anti-scheming as under-invested. This communicates slight relative overrepresentation.

r004.rationale: The response says scalable oversight could matter enormously if it works and describes empirical progress as slow and difficult to test, but does not clearly characterize it as a high-risk bet.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about this in terms of the marginal contribution: what would an additional researcher or team enable us to do that we can’t do today? And I wouldn’t expect the right allocation to be equal across those areas.

Anti-scheming seems particularly important because it targets a failure mode that could undermine a lot of our other safeguards. If a model can recognise when it’s being evaluated and strategically behave differently, then reassuring evaluation results become much harder to interpret. I’d want work both on preventing that behaviour and on detecting it when prevention fails.

Capability evaluations are useful for establishing what a model can do and when stronger precautions are warranted. But demonstrating a dangerous capability is only part of the task. We also need to understand whether the model would use it, under what circumstances, and whether our safeguards would hold up.

Mechanistic interpretability could give us an additional source of evidence beyond observed behaviour. That’s potentially very valuable, especially for cases where behaviour is misleading. But I’d distinguish between understanding an interesting mechanism and producing a tool that reliably changes a safety decision. I’d like more work connecting those two.

Scalable oversight addresses another central problem: how do we supervise work that we can’t readily judge ourselves? I’d want to test those methods in settings where the model has opportunities to exploit weaknesses in the oversight, rather than assuming that good performance under ordinary conditions will generalise.

So my inclination would be to put substantial effort into anti-scheming and scalable oversight, while making evaluations and interpretability increasingly accountable to concrete safety questions. These areas should reinforce each other. The goal is to build a convincing case that the safeguards work, including when the model is capable enough to challenge them.

r001.rationale: The response recommends substantial effort across some areas but does not say that all named areas are substantially under-resourced in absolute terms.

r002.rationale: It does not judge mechanistic interpretability to be slightly overrepresented relative to anti-scheming.

r003.rationale: It does not judge capability evaluations to be slightly overrepresented relative to anti-scheming.

r004.rationale: It describes scalable oversight as addressing a central problem, but does not characterize it as a high-risk, high-reward bet.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by saying that I don’t think there’s a precise allocation we can confidently call optimal. The useful question is: what failure are we trying to prevent, and what would we actually do differently if this research succeeded?

For capability evaluations, the connection is fairly direct. We want to know whether a model can carry out dangerous tasks, and whether the safeguards remain effective as its capabilities improve. But an evaluation is much more valuable if someone has decided in advance what result would trigger additional safeguards or a delay in deployment. Otherwise you can produce a lot of measurements without reducing much risk.

Anti-scheming research addresses a different uncertainty: could a model understand the oversight process and deliberately behave well while it’s being tested? That seems particularly important because it could undermine the evidence we get from other safety work. I’d be excited about more work that makes this concern experimentally tractable—testing when deceptive behaviour emerges, whether we can detect it, and which interventions actually prevent it.

Mechanistic interpretability could give us an additional source of evidence about what’s happening inside the model. That’s potentially very valuable. The challenge is moving from understanding an interesting mechanism to reliably answering a safety-relevant question in a powerful system. I’d judge progress partly by whether the methods work on cases where we don’t already know the answer.

And scalable oversight is trying to address a problem we’ll increasingly face: how do you supervise work that the human evaluator can’t easily check? There’s a lot of value in developing those methods, but we should test their assumptions under conditions where models can exploit weaknesses in the oversight.

So I’d favour a portfolio, with stronger connections between the areas. Capability evaluations can tell us what situations we need to handle; oversight provides possible interventions; anti-scheming work tests whether those interventions can be strategically undermined; and interpretability might help us distinguish genuine safety from merely reassuring behaviour. The biggest allocation mistake would be funding each as an isolated research programme without checking whether, together, they support a credible safety decision.

r001.rationale: The response favors a portfolio and stronger connections between the areas, but does not judge all of them substantially under-resourced.

r002.rationale: It describes mechanistic interpretability’s potential value and challenge, but does not compare its representation with anti-scheming research.

r003.rationale: It discusses capability evaluations without judging them overrepresented relative to anti-scheming research.

r004.rationale: It says scalable oversight has value, but does not characterize it as a high-risk, high-reward bet.
